title: The doorpost
hook: touching the mezuzah on the way out
tomorrow: the broken tablets went into the Ark. why keep broken pieces?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a week of careful speech: no lashon hara, even when it's true. Seven days of clean speech. Today, words that never leave the door.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS OF CLEAN SPEECH.` → `WORDS ON THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The third squad of soldiers has one order: don't talk to him. Not a word. The emperor sent two squads before this one to bring in Onkelos, a Roman who became a Jew, and both times Onkelos talked with them until they became Jews too. So this squad leads him out of his house in silence. At the door, Onkelos stops and puts his hand on a small case fixed to the doorpost. Then he asks them: what is this? The soldiers have been warned. But they're curious. You tell us, they say.
screen: `ORDERS: DON'T TALK TO HIM.` → `TWO SQUADS ALREADY WON OVER.` → `HIS HAND ON THE DOORPOST.`

segments.voice: So he tells them. In this world, a king sits inside, and his servants stand outside to guard him. With the Holy One it's the other way around: His servants sit inside, and He guards them from outside. Then he quotes a Psalm: the LORD guards your going out and your coming in. The soldiers, the Talmud says, became Jews too, and the emperor sent no more. So what was under his hand? Deuteronomy says it plainly: "And thou shalt write them upon the door-posts of thy house, and upon thy gates." Write what? The words just before, the Shema: hear, O Israel, and love the LORD with all your heart. The Hebrew for doorposts is mezuzot, so the little case carries the doorpost's own name: mezuzah. Inside is a scribe's parchment with those paragraphs. And notice where it hangs. Not on the desk where you study, not by the bed. On the threshold, where you leave. The words are posted at the exit so they go out with you: into the street, the job, the argument. Some people touch it on every pass and kiss their fingers. Onkelos touched it on his way to being arrested. Something to tell a friend tonight: the mezuzah is named after the doorpost itself.
screen: `THE KING IS GUARDED; HERE GOD GUARDS.` · `WRITE THEM ON YOUR DOORPOSTS.` · `MEZUZAH: THE DOORPOST'S OWN NAME.` · `POSTED AT THE EXIT.` · then, large: `CARRY THE WORDS OUT.`

segments.voice: Stand up and walk slowly to the nearest doorway. Rest your fingertips on the frame for a moment, the way people touch a mezuzah on the way out, and feel the wood or the paint. Then step through, unhurried, as though you're carrying something with you.
screen: `WALK TO THE DOOR.` · `FINGERTIPS ON THE FRAME.` · `STEP THROUGH, CARRYING IT.`

segments.voice: The doorpost: where the mezuzah hangs, holding the Shema's words, touched on the way in and the way out.
Here's the line: carry the words out. The doorpost is where they leave the house with you.

screen: `DAY 1660 COUNTS.` → `A RULE OF LIFE · 13 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: WHY KEEP THE BROKEN TABLETS?`

howItsDone: Jewish homes fix a mezuzah, a case holding a handwritten parchment of the Shema's paragraphs, on the right-hand doorpost of the entrance and often on inner doors; many people touch it, and some kiss their fingers, as they pass.

chat.meaning: The mezuzah hangs on the threshold so the Shema's words go out with you. Every going out counts, even a trash run.
